concepts.coreInsight_ar: صرخة 'يا ليتني لم أوت كتابيه' تكشف ندماً ساحقاً - متمنياً التراجع عما لا يمكن التراجع عنه، عدم رؤية ما لا يمكن عدم رؤيته.
concepts.whyItMatters_ar: هذا الندم المدمر يجب أن يحفزنا على العيش بمساءلة الآن، حتى لا نواجه أبداً هذه اللحظة من الندم غير القابل للعكس.

concepts.title: Wishing Blindness
concepts.coreInsight: The sinner wishes they had never received their record at all - preferring ignorance over the painful truth of their failures.
concepts.whyItMatters: This teaches us that truth, though sometimes painful now, is better faced in this life where repentance is possible.
concepts.coreInsight_urdu: گناہ گار کی خواہش ہے کہ کاش اسے اپنا نامہ اعمال ملتا ہی نہ - اپنی ناکامیوں کی دردناک سچائی سے لاعلمی کو ترجیح دیتا ہے۔
concepts.whyItMatters_urdu: یہ سکھاتا ہے کہ سچائی، اگرچہ ابھی تکلیف دہ ہو، اس زندگی میں بہتر ہے جہاں توبہ ممکن ہے۔
concepts.coreInsight_ar: الخاطئ يتمنى أنه لم يتلق سجله على الإطلاق - مفضلاً الجهل على الحقيقة المؤلمة لإخفاقاته.
concepts.whyItMatters_ar: هذا يعلمنا أن الحقيقة، رغم أنها مؤلمة أحياناً الآن، من الأفضل مواجهتها في هذه الحياة حيث التوبة ممكنة.

25.layer4: Both Shia and Sunni scholars interpret this verse as describing the anguish of those who receive their records in the left hand, facing damnation for their sins. Sunni exegetes like Ibn Kathir and Tabari explain that the left hand indicates rejection and entry into Hellfire, contrasting with the right hand that indicates acceptance and Paradise. Qurtubi emphasizes that the desperate wish reflects complete hopelessness and regret when facing the consequences of a misspent life. Sunni tradition generally interprets those receiving records in the left hand as disbelievers and severe sinners whose evil deeds outweighed their good. Shia scholarship agrees with the fundamental interpretation but places particular emphasis on those who rejected the divinely appointed Imams and opposed the Ahlul Bayt. Tabrisi in Majma al-Bayan presents traditions specifically linking this category to enemies of Imam Ali and those who usurped the rights of the Prophet's family. This represents an interpretive difference, with Shia exegesis seeing particular historical and doctrinal dimensions. Both traditions agree that this verse serves as a serious warning to examine one's life and make corrections before it is too late. The shared message is that the time for action is now, before the Day when only regret remains.
25.layer4_urdu: شیعہ اور اہل سنت کے علما اس عذاب پر متفق ہیں۔ ابن کثیر تفصیل دیتے ہیں۔ دونوں روایات بیان کرتی ہیں کہ یہ نہ کریں۔
25.layer4_ar: يتفق علماء الشيعة والسنة على تفسير هذه الآية بوصفها صارخةً بالأسى الذي يعتري من يتسلَّمون كتبهم بالشمال أمام الهلاك الأبدي جراء ذنوبهم. فمفسِّرو أهل السنة كابن كثير والطبري يُبيِّنون أن الشمال يدلُّ على الردِّ والدخول في النار، مقابل اليمين التي تدلُّ على القبول والجنة. ويُؤكِّد القرطبي أن هذا التمنِّي الحارق يعكس يأساً كاملاً وندماً مضنياً حين يواجه المرء عواقب حياة أُهدرت. ويفسِّر التراث السني في الغالب هذه الفئة بالكافرين والعصاة الشديدي الإجرام ممن رجحت سيِّئاتهم على حسناتهم. ويتفق التراث الشيعي مع التفسير الجوهري مع تركيز خاص على من رفضوا الأئمة الربانيين وعارضوا أهل البيت. والشيخ الطبرسي في مجمع البيان يُورد روايات تربط هذه الفئة تحديداً بأعداء الإمام علي ومن اغتصبوا حق آل النبي. وهذا يُمثِّل فارقاً تفسيرياً إذ يرى التفسير الشيعي أبعاداً تاريخية وعقدية بعينها. ويتفق التراثان على أن الآية تنهض إنذاراً جاداً للمرء بمراجعة حياته وتصحيح مسارها قبل فوات الأوان. والرسالة المشتركة أن وقت العمل الآن قبل ذلك اليوم الذي لا يبقى فيه إلا الندم.
25.layer1: Verse twenty-five begins the second portrait in the surah's great human division, and it opens with a devastating contrast to verse nineteen. Where verse nineteen showed a person receiving their record in their right hand with a cry of triumph and invitation, verse twenty-five shows a person receiving their record in their left hand with a cry of anguish and despair: 'But as for him who is given his record in his left hand, he will say: Oh, I wish I had not been given my record.' The left hand in Quranic symbolism is the hand of dishonour, of rejected offering, of that which does not receive the mark of divine approval. Just as the right hand signalled before the record was even read that the outcome was good, the left hand signals that the outcome is catastrophic. The expression ya laytani, 'oh would that I,' is a formula of intense, impossible wishing in Arabic. It is the language not of complaint but of total helplessness in the face of irreversible reality. The person does not say 'I wish things were different' as a mild preference; they say ya laytani with the full weight of a desperate soul that has nothing left but the wish that the record did not exist. Lam utah kitabiyah, 'I had not been given my record,' means the person wishes for the impossible: that the accounting had never happened, that the record never existed, that they could step back behind the curtain of their own deeds. But the record is in their hands. It is real, it is complete, it is irrefutable. Every omission of prayer, every act of injustice, every moment of arrogance, every truth they suppressed, every heedlessness they nursed, is there. And there is nothing to be done about it. The practical lesson this verse teaches those who are still in this world is precisely that there is still something to be done: repent, change, act. The person of verse twenty-five no longer has that option. The person reading this verse still does.
25.layer2: Ibn Kathir, in Tafsir al-Quran al-Azim, explains that the giving of the record in the left hand is established across multiple hadith traditions as the mark of the condemned. He notes that several narrations describe the giving of the records on the Day of Judgment in detail, and that the universal indicator among the authentic hadith is that the righteous receive their books from their right side or from in front of them, while the condemned receive them from behind their backs into their left hands, as confirmed by the following verse in this surah. Ibn Kathir elaborates that the desperate cry ya laytani lam utah kitabiyah represents the person's final recognition of their total failure: they cannot dispute the record, cannot offer alternative evidence, cannot plead ignorance, because the record is complete and before them. He cites Ibn Abbas's explanation that the 'record' includes not only actions but words, intentions, and even the thoughts that were entertained and acted upon, making it a comprehensive archive of everything the person was responsible for. Al-Tabari, in Jami al-Bayan, records the view of Qatadah that the expression ya laytani means the person wishes they had been given no record at all, had never existed, had never had a soul capable of choice and accountability. Tabari notes that this is the ultimate expression of regret: wishing not merely for a different outcome but for non-existence itself. Al-Qurtubi, in Al-Jami li-Ahkam al-Quran, notes the structural parallel between verse nineteen and verse twenty-five: both begin with the same grammatical construction describing the person receiving the record, and both give voice to the person's immediate verbal response. The parallel is deliberately ironic: the same moment, the same act of receiving the book, produces the most ecstatic announcement in one person and the most desperate lament in the other. The determining factor is not the moment but the lifetime that preceded it.
25.layer3: Wahbah al-Zuhayli, in Al-Tafsir al-Munir, focuses on the rhetorical and structural function of verse twenty-five within the surah. He notes that the surah has spent verses nineteen through twenty-four painting an extraordinarily vivid and warm picture of the person of the right hand, immersed in pleasant life, an elevated garden, near fruit, and divine invitation to feast. The abrupt shift in verse twenty-five, introduced by the Arabic particle wa-amma meaning 'but as for,' forces the listener to confront the full contrast: everything described in verses twenty-one through twenty-four belongs to one group, and this group, the people of the left hand, will experience none of it. Al-Zuhayli argues that this juxtaposition is the surah's most powerful rhetorical device, because it makes the stakes of the choice absolutely concrete. The choice between the right hand and the left hand is not an abstract theological matter; it is the choice between the feast of verses twenty-one through twenty-four and the anguish of verse twenty-five. Sayyid Qutb, in Fi Zilal al-Quran, writes with deep psychological insight that the cry ya laytani lam utah kitabiyah is the Quran's portrait of what he calls the moment of ultimate truth: the moment when a person who spent their life in a particular relationship to reality, ignoring its divine dimension, is finally confronted with that reality in its complete and irrefutable form. He argues that this moment is the logical consequence of living without zannantu, without the living certainty of verse twenty: the person who did not carry the certainty of accountability in their heart during life now faces that accountability without any preparation. Sheikh Ibn Uthaymeen, in his commentary, drew the stark practical lesson that the difference between verse nineteen and verse twenty-five is constructed across a lifetime of small daily choices. He urged believers to regularly ask themselves which portrait they are building toward, and to make corrections immediately rather than accumulating the deeds that lead to the desperate cry of verse twenty-five.

concepts.title: Willful Ignorance
concepts.coreInsight: The lament 'had not known what is my account' reveals how the sinner lived in deliberate ignorance, avoiding thoughts of accountability.
concepts.whyItMatters: Living in denial of the Day of Judgment is a form of self-deception - we must confront this reality to live authentically.
concepts.coreInsight_urdu: 'کاش میں اپنے حساب کو نہ جانتا' کا نوحہ ظاہر کرتا ہے کہ گناہ گار جان بوجھ کر لاعلمی میں زندگی گزارتا تھا، جوابدہی کے خیالات سے بچتا تھا۔
concepts.whyItMatters_urdu: یوم قیامت کے انکار میں زندگی گزارنا خود فریبی کی ایک شکل ہے - ہمیں اس حقیقت کا سامنا کرنا چاہیے تاکہ سچی زندگی گزار سکیں۔
concepts.coreInsight_ar: النواح 'ولم أدر ما حسابيه' يكشف كيف عاش الخاطئ في جهل متعمد، متجنباً أفكار المساءلة.
concepts.whyItMatters_ar: العيش في إنكار يوم القيامة هو شكل من أشكال خداع الذات - يجب أن نواجه هذا الواقع للعيش بصدق.

concepts.title: Avoided Truth
concepts.coreInsight: The phrase 'had not known' (lam adri) suggests the person could have known but chose not to - they avoided warnings and reminders.
concepts.whyItMatters: We are responsible for seeking truth, not avoiding it - ignoring warnings doesn't absolve us of accountability.
concepts.coreInsight_urdu: 'نہ جانتا' کا جملہ بتاتا ہے کہ شخص جان سکتا تھا لیکن نہیں جاننا چاہا - اس نے تنبیہات اور یاد دہانیوں سے گریز کیا۔
concepts.whyItMatters_urdu: ہم سچائی تلاش کرنے کے ذمہ دار ہیں، اس سے بچنے کے نہیں - تنبیہات کو نظر انداز کرنا ہمیں جوابدہی سے بری نہیں کرتا۔
concepts.coreInsight_ar: عبارة 'لم أدر' يشير إلى أن الشخص كان يمكنه أن يعرف لكنه اختار عدم المعرفة - تجنب التحذيرات والتذكيرات.
concepts.whyItMatters_ar: نحن مسؤولون عن السعي للحقيقة، وليس تجنبها - تجاهل التحذيرات لا يعفينا من المساءلة.

concepts.title: Reckoning Shock
concepts.coreInsight: The shock of confronting the 'account' (hisab) reveals that many live as if judgment is theoretical, not an absolute certainty they will face.
concepts.whyItMatters: Making the Day of Reckoning real in our minds transforms it from abstract theology to concrete motivation for righteous living.
concepts.coreInsight_urdu: 'حساب' کا سامنا کرنے کا صدمہ ظاہر کرتا ہے کہ بہت سے لوگ ایسے جیتے ہیں جیسے فیصلہ نظریاتی ہے، نہ کہ ایک مطلق یقینی جس کا وہ سامنا کریں گے۔
concepts.whyItMatters_urdu: حساب کے دن کو اپنے ذہنوں میں حقیقی بنانا اسے خلاصہ الہیات سے نیک زندگی کے لیے ٹھوس محرک میں بدل دیتا ہے۔
concepts.coreInsight_ar: صدمة مواجهة 'الحساب' تكشف أن كثيرين يعيشون كما لو أن الحساب نظري، وليس يقيناً مطلقاً سيواجهونه.
concepts.whyItMatters_ar: جعل يوم الحساب حقيقياً في أذهاننا يحوله من لاهوت مجرد إلى حافز ملموس للعيش الصالح.

26.layer4: Both Shia and Sunni scholars interpret this verse as expressing the desperate regret of those facing damnation, wishing they could return to ignorance about their fate. Sunni exegetes like Ibn Kathir explain that the wish to have never known the accounting reflects the severity of the punishment they face and their recognition that there is no escape. Qurtubi and Tabari emphasize that this represents complete hopelessness, as the person sees no way to improve their situation and wishes only for unconsciousness or non-existence. Fakhr al-Din al-Razi discusses the philosophical dimensions of knowledge and suffering, noting that awareness of eternal torment is itself a form of torment. Shia scholarship agrees with these interpretations while adding emphasis on the special regret of those who had access to the teachings of the Ahlul Bayt but rejected them. Allamah Tabatabai in Al-Mizan discusses how different levels of knowledge create different levels of responsibility and accountability. Tabrisi in Majma al-Bayan presents traditions about specific groups whose knowledge will become a source of torment rather than salvation. Both traditions use this verse to warn believers to act upon the knowledge they have, ensuring that awareness of truth becomes a blessing rather than a curse. The shared message is that knowing truth without acting on it may be worse than ignorance.
26.layer4_urdu: شیعہ اور اہل سنت کے علما اس پشتاوے پر متفق ہیں۔ ابن کثیر تفصیل دیتے ہیں۔ دونوں روایات بیان کرتی ہیں کہ اب بہت دیر ہے۔
26.layer4_ar: يتفق علماء الشيعة والسنة على تفسير هذه الآية بوصفها تعبيراً عن حسرة يائسة تعتري المحكوم عليهم بالعذاب، إذ يتمنَّون لو عادوا إلى الجهل بمصيرهم. فمفسِّرو أهل السنة كابن كثير يُبيِّنون أن تمنِّي الجهل بالحساب يكشف شدَّة العقاب الذي ينتظرهم وإدراكهم أنه لا فكاك منه. ويُؤكِّد القرطبي والطبري أن هذا يُمثِّل يأساً مطلقاً إذ لا يرى المرء مخرجاً وتمنَّى فحسب اللاوعي أو العدم. وفخر الدين الرازي يُناقش الأبعاد الفلسفية للعلم والمعاناة مُشيراً إلى أن الوعي بالعذاب الأبدي هو ذاته ضرب من العذاب. ويتفق التراث الشيعي مع هذه التفسيرات مضيفاً تأكيداً خاصاً على حسرة من توافر لهم الوصول إلى تعاليم أهل البيت عليهم السلام ثم أعرضوا عنها. والعلامة الطباطبائي في الميزان يُناقش كيف تُنشئ درجات العلم المختلفة درجات متفاوتة من المسؤولية والمحاسبة. والشيخ الطبرسي في مجمع البيان يُورد روايات في فئات بعينها سيكون علمها مصدر عذاب لا نجاة. ويتفق التراثان في توظيف هذه الآية للحثِّ على العمل بالعلم المتاح ضماناً لأن يكون الوعي بالحق نعمةً لا نقمة. والرسالة المشتركة أن علم الحق دون العمل به قد يكون أوخم عاقبةً من الجهل.
26.layer1: Verse twenty-six continues the anguished lament of the person who received their record in their left hand. Having cried out in verse twenty-five that they wished the record had never been given to them, they now add a second devastating confession: 'And had not known what is my account.' The phrase wa lam adri ma hisabiyah carries enormous theological weight. In Arabic, adri means to know through awareness, attention, and engagement. The person is not confessing that they were never told about accountability; the prophets and messengers had brought the message and the warnings were clear. Rather, they are confessing that they never truly absorbed it, never allowed it to become real to them, never carried the knowledge of their account as a living reality that shaped their choices. This is the spiritual condition that classical scholars call ghafla, heedlessness: not total ignorance but practical unawareness, the state of knowing about the Hereafter without it mattering to the way one lives. The word hisabiyah, my account, ends with the familiar breathy pause marker h, creating the same rhyme as kitabiyah in verse twenty-five, and will echo again in verse twenty-seven and the following verses, tying the lament together into a cohesive sequence of regret. The practical implication for every believer reading this verse is urgent and direct: the time to know your account is now, in this life, while the account is still open and amendable. The person of verse twenty-six never confronted what their account was building toward. The person reading this verse still has the ability to look honestly at what they are putting forward and to change it. The contrast between the believer's zannantu in verse twenty and this person's lam adri in verse twenty-six is the contrast between two lives: one lived in conscious awareness of divine accountability and one lived in practical denial of it.
26.layer2: Ibn Kathir, in Tafsir al-Quran al-Azim, offers two possible interpretations of the phrase wa lam adri ma hisabiyah. The first is that the person is expressing the magnitude of the reckoning: the accounting is so severe and so comprehensive that they feel they had never truly understood what a reckoning was, had never imagined it could be so thorough and so final. On this reading, the verse expresses shock at the completeness of divine justice rather than a confession of negligence. The second interpretation, which Ibn Kathir presents as consistent with the context, is that the person confesses to having lived without genuine attention to their account: they never took the hisab seriously during their lifetime, never reflected on what they were accumulating, never measured their deeds against the standard of divine justice. Al-Tabari, in Jami al-Bayan, records from Qatadah the view that this verse describes someone who deliberately avoided thinking about accountability, and that the Quran here shows that such avoidance does not eliminate the account but only ensures that when the account arrives it arrives as a complete shock. Al-Tabari himself notes that the sequential structure of verse twenty-five and verse twenty-six is deliberate: first the wish that the record had not been given, then the confession that the account was never truly known. These are two dimensions of the same spiritual failure: the person neither accepted the record nor engaged with the reality that the record was being kept. Al-Qurtubi, in Al-Jami li-Ahkam al-Quran, draws the legal and ethical lesson that every Muslim has an obligation to engage in muhasaba, self-accounting, during their lifetime, and that verse twenty-six is the Quranic proof that failing to practise muhasaba in this world means encountering one's account for the first time on the Day of Judgment under the worst possible conditions. Fakhr al-Din al-Razi, in Mafatih al-Ghayb, notes the philosophical dimension: knowledge without action is a form of non-knowledge from the perspective of spiritual development, and the person who knew about hisab but did not live in its light did not truly know it.
26.layer3: Wahbah al-Zuhayli, in Al-Tafsir al-Munir, reads verse twenty-six as the Quran's most concise diagnosis of the spiritual disease that leads to the left-hand record. The disease is not wickedness in the dramatic sense but rather a chronic failure of attention: the person never made the hisab real in their inner life. Al-Zuhayli connects this to the broader Quranic concept of tafakkur, reflection and contemplation, arguing that verse twenty-six is what happens when tafakkur is abandoned across a lifetime. The person was perhaps not a deliberate wrongdoer; they were a person who simply never paused to genuinely ask what their account was accumulating and what it was moving toward. In an age of relentless distraction and entertainment, Al-Zuhayli observes, this is the most common form of spiritual failure in the contemporary Muslim world: not explicit rejection of the faith but gradual practical heedlessness in which the Hereafter recedes from consciousness until it exerts no real influence over daily choices. Sayyid Qutb, in Fi Zilal al-Quran, writes that the phrase lam adri ma hisabiyah is the Quran's portrait of a life lived without the dimension of eternity. He argues that every human life is either lived with eternity in view, which produces the zannantu of verse twenty, or without eternity in view, which produces the lam adri of verse twenty-six. There is no neutral ground: either the hisab is a living reality that shapes choices or it is not, and if it is not, then the person is accumulating an account they will encounter for the first time under conditions of irreversible judgment. Sheikh Ibn Uthaymeen, in his commentary on the shorter eschatological surahs, recommended the daily practice of muhasaba before sleep as the specific Sunnah remedy for the spiritual condition described in verse twenty-six, citing the counsel of Umar ibn al-Khattab that a person should take account of themselves before they are taken to account.

concepts.title: Wishing Annihilation
concepts.coreInsight: The cry 'I wish my death had been the decisive one' expresses desperation for non-existence - preferring annihilation over eternal torment.
concepts.whyItMatters: This extreme regret shows that temporary worldly pleasures are never worth eternal consequences - we must prioritize the lasting over the fleeting.
concepts.coreInsight_urdu: 'کاش میری موت حتمی ہوتی' کی پکار نابودگی کی مایوسی کا اظہار ہے - ابدی عذاب سے بہتر نابودگی کو ترجیح دینا۔
concepts.whyItMatters_urdu: یہ انتہائی پچھتاوا دکھاتا ہے کہ عارضی دنیاوی لذتیں کبھی ابدی نتائج کے قابل نہیں - ہمیں عارضی پر دائمی کو ترجیح دینی چاہیے۔
concepts.coreInsight_ar: صرخة 'يا ليتها كانت القاضية' تعبر عن يأس للعدم - مفضلاً الفناء على العذاب الأبدي.
concepts.whyItMatters_ar: هذا الندم الشديد يظهر أن الملذات الدنيوية المؤقتة لا تستحق أبداً العواقب الأبدية - يجب أن نعطي الأولوية للدائم على العابر.

concepts.title: Ultimate Finality
concepts.coreInsight: The term 'decisive' (qadiya) means 'the ending', wishing that physical death had been the absolute end with no resurrection or accountability.
concepts.whyItMatters: This verse refutes materialist denial of afterlife - resurrection is real, and we must prepare for it rather than wish it away.
concepts.coreInsight_urdu: 'فیصلہ کن' کا مطلب ہے 'اختتام'، یہ خواہش کہ جسمانی موت مطلق اختتام ہوتی بغیر جی اٹھنے یا جوابدہی کے۔
concepts.whyItMatters_urdu: یہ آیت آخرت کے مادیت پسندانہ انکار کو رد کرتی ہے - جی اٹھنا حقیقت ہے، اور ہمیں اس کے لیے تیار ہونا چاہیے نہ کہ اسے ختم کرنے کی خواہش کریں۔
concepts.coreInsight_ar: مصطلح 'القاضية' يعني 'النهاية'، متمنياً أن يكون الموت الجسدي النهاية المطلقة بلا بعث أو مساءلة.
concepts.whyItMatters_ar: هذه الآية تدحض الإنكار المادي للآخرة - البعث حقيقي، ويجب أن نستعد له بدلاً من تمني زواله.

concepts.title: No Second Chance
concepts.coreInsight: The desperate wish reveals the finality of judgment - no return, no second chance, no ability to undo what has been done.
concepts.whyItMatters: Since there are no do-overs after death, we must seize the opportunity for repentance and reform while we still live.
concepts.coreInsight_urdu: مایوس خواہش فیصلے کی حتمیت کو ظاہر کرتی ہے - کوئی واپسی نہیں، کوئی دوسرا موقع نہیں، جو ہو گیا اسے ختم کرنے کی کوئی صلاحیت نہیں۔
concepts.whyItMatters_urdu: چونکہ موت کے بعد کوئی دوبارہ موقع نہیں، ہمیں توبہ اور اصلاح کا موقع پکڑنا چاہیے جب ہم ابھی زندہ ہیں۔
concepts.coreInsight_ar: الأمنية اليائسة تكشف نهائية الحكم - لا عودة، لا فرصة ثانية، لا قدرة على التراجع عما تم.
concepts.whyItMatters_ar: بما أنه لا توجد إعادات بعد الموت، يجب أن نغتنم فرصة التوبة والإصلاح بينما لا نزال أحياء.

27.layer4: Both Shia and Sunni scholars interpret this verse as expressing the ultimate despair of those facing eternal damnation. Sunni exegetes like Ibn Kathir and Tabari explain that the wish for death to have been final reflects the severity of the torment the person faces in the Hereafter, making non-existence seem preferable. Qurtubi emphasizes that this represents complete hopelessness, as the person realizes their suffering will never end and they can never escape. Sunni tradition generally applies this to disbelievers and severe sinners facing Hellfire. Shia scholarship agrees with the fundamental interpretation while placing particular emphasis on those who opposed the rightful Imams and led others astray. Allamah Tabatabai in Al-Mizan discusses the philosophical dimensions of existence and non-existence, noting that the wish for non-existence reveals that the person's existence has become purely negative, consisting only of suffering without any positive element. Tabrisi in Majma al-Bayan presents traditions from the Ahlul Bayt about specific categories of people who will express this wish, particularly oppressive leaders and those who actively fought against truth. Both traditions agree that this verse serves as the most serious warning to examine our lives and make corrections before facing this irreversible fate. The shared message is that the purpose of life is to prepare for eternity, and failure in this purpose leads to the ultimate regret.
27.layer4_urdu: شیعہ اور اہل سنت کے علما اس خواہش پر متفق ہیں۔ ابن کثیر تفصیل دیتے ہیں۔ دونوں روایات بیان کرتی ہیں کہ یہ خوفناک ہے۔
27.layer4_ar: يتفق علماء الشيعة والسنة على تفسير هذه الآية بوصفها تعبيراً عن اليأس المطلق لمن يواجهون الخلود في العذاب. فمفسِّرو أهل السنة كابن كثير والطبري يُبيِّنون أن تمنِّي أن تكون الموتة قاضيةً يكشف شدَّة العذاب الذي يلقاه هذا الشخص في الآخرة حتى يُفضِّل العدم عليه. ويُؤكِّد القرطبي أن هذا يُمثِّل يأساً مطلقاً إذ يُدرك المرء أن معاناته لن تنقطع وأنه لا ملاذ له. ويُناقش العلامة الطباطبائي في الميزان الأبعاد الفلسفية للوجود والعدم مُلاحِظاً أن تمنِّي العدم يُنبئ بأن وجود الشخص صار سلبياً محضاً لا يتكوَّن إلا من معاناة خالية من أي بُعد إيجابي. والشيخ الطبرسي في مجمع البيان يُورد روايات عن أهل البيت في فئات بعينها ستُعبِّر عن هذا التمنِّي، ولا سيَّما القادة الظالمون والمتآمرون على الحق. وتُضيف الدراسات الشيعية تأكيداً خاصاً على من عارضوا الأئمة الشرعيين وأضلُّوا الأمة عن الصراط المستقيم. ويتفق التراثان على أن الآية تقدِّم أبلغ إنذار بمراجعة الحياة وتصحيح المسار قبل هذا المصير الذي لا رجعة عنه. والرسالة المشتركة أن الغرض من الحياة هو الاستعداد للأبدية وأن الإخفاق في هذا الغرض يُفضي إلى أعمق الندم.
27.layer1: Verse twenty-seven represents the third and most extreme wish in the condemned person's sequence of desperate laments. Having wished in verse twenty-five that the record had never been given to them, and having confessed in verse twenty-six that they never truly knew their account, the person now utters a wish that strikes at the deepest level of human existential dread: 'Oh, I wish my death had been the decisive one.' The Arabic ya laytaha kanat al-qadiya is a cry of the most intense desperation. The word qadiya comes from qada, meaning to decide, to settle finally, to put an end to something permanently. The person is wishing that the death they experienced in this world had been truly final, permanently settling their existence by ending it altogether. This is a wish for non-existence, for annihilation, for the complete erasure of the self rather than facing the eternal consequences that now await. Scholars note that this wish is impossible not only practically but conceptually: the soul does not cease to exist after physical death, and the very fact that this person is crying out this wish proves that existence continues. The wish for al-qadiya, the decisive end, is thus a wish that contradicts the very condition in which it is uttered. The verse teaches believers something of incalculable importance: whatever discomforts, trials, and hardships exist in this life, they are finite. There will come a moment when they end. The punishment of the Hereafter has no such moment. The person who wishes for annihilation in verse twenty-seven is reaching for the mercy of finitude, of limitation, of ending, and finding that such mercy is no longer available. This is the ultimate practical argument for taking the Hereafter seriously in this life: the stakes are not temporary but permanent, and permanent suffering is of an entirely different order of gravity than any suffering this world can produce.
27.layer2: Ibn Kathir, in Tafsir al-Quran al-Azim, explains that the word al-qadiya in this verse refers to a death that would have been absolute and final, meaning a death with no resurrection. The condemned person is wishing that they had simply ceased to exist at the moment of their worldly death and had not been brought back for the accounting. Ibn Kathir notes the contrast between this wish and the Islamic understanding of death: in Islam, death is not an end but a transition, and the wish for death as final annihilation reflects the materialist worldview that the condemned had embraced in their earthly life coming back to mock them. Those who denied the resurrection in this world now wish with all their being that the resurrection they denied were indeed false. Al-Tabari, in Jami al-Bayan, records from Qatadah that the phrase ya laytaha kanat al-qadiya means the person wishes their first death, the death of this world, had been the death that cut off all further existence. Tabari preserves the view of several Successors that al-qadiya specifically refers to a death that terminates the person's very being, leaving no remnant for resurrection or judgment. He notes that this wish is psychologically consistent with the sequence of the preceding verses: having wished the record did not exist and having confessed to never truly engaging with the hisab, the person now wishes for the most extreme possible escape, the abolition of their own existence. Al-Qurtubi, in Al-Jami li-Ahkam al-Quran, notes that this verse provides strong Quranic evidence for the reality of the resurrection, because the condemned person wishes specifically that death had been final and that no resurrection had occurred, which implicitly confirms that a resurrection has in fact taken place. The condemned are not confused about whether they are resurrected; they are in agony about it and wishing it were otherwise. Fakhr al-Din al-Razi uses this verse in his theological discussions to argue that the wish for annihilation on the Day of Judgment is itself evidence that the Day has genuine experiential content and that its sufferings are real and consciously experienced.
27.layer3: Wahbah al-Zuhayli, in Al-Tafsir al-Munir, situates this verse as the emotional and rhetorical climax of the condemned person's self-expression in the surah. He observes that verses twenty-five, twenty-six, and twenty-seven form a three-step sequence of escalating despair: wish for the record to be absent, confession of never having engaged with the account, and finally wish for total annihilation. Each step is more extreme than the last, and together they paint a portrait of a soul that has run out of options and has nothing left but impossible wishes. Al-Zuhayli draws the contemporary application that the popularity of materialist and atheist worldviews in the modern era, which promise exactly what this person wishes for, namely that death is final and there is no accounting, represents not intellectual freedom but the adoption of a false comfort. The person of verse twenty-seven discovers on the Day of Judgment that the materialist comfort they embraced in this world was a lie, and the discovery comes too late. Sayyid Qutb, in Fi Zilal al-Quran, writes with great intensity about this verse, calling it the Quran's most honest portrait of what it feels like to be trapped in existence without hope. He argues that the wish ya laytaha kanat al-qadiya is not merely dramatic poetry but a precise description of the experiential condition of a soul that has lost access to mercy and can see no exit. He connects this to the famous hadith in Sahih Muslim in which the people of Hell are told they will neither live fully nor die, and he argues that verse twenty-seven gives the human interior of that hadith: to be in existence without the possibility of relief is the ultimate suffering. Sheikh Ibn Uthaymeen observed that verse twenty-seven should be read alongside the Quranic descriptions of the people who will say in Hell 'call upon your Lord to end our lives,' and that together these texts teach believers to view the mercy of mortality, of limitation, of endings, as a tremendous divine gift that will be withdrawn forever at the moment of final judgment.

concepts.title: Worthless Wealth
concepts.coreInsight: The cry 'My wealth has not availed me' reveals the ultimate futility of material accumulation - riches cannot buy salvation or escape from divine justice.
concepts.whyItMatters: This stark reality should transform how we view and use wealth, prioritizing what we send forward over what we accumulate.
concepts.coreInsight_urdu: 'میری دولت نے مجھے کوئی فائدہ نہیں دیا' کی پکار مادی جمع کرنے کی حتمی بے سودگی کو ظاہر کرتی ہے - دولت نجات نہیں خرید سکتی۔
concepts.whyItMatters_urdu: یہ واضح حقیقت ہمارے نظریے اور دولت کے استعمال کو بدل دینی چاہیے، جو ہم جمع کرتے ہیں اس پر جو آگے بھیجتے ہیں اسے ترجیح دیں۔
concepts.coreInsight_ar: صرخة 'ما أغنى عني ماليه' تكشف عبث التراكم المادي - الثروة لا يمكنها شراء الخلاص أو الهروب من العدل الإلهي.
concepts.whyItMatters_ar: هذا الواقع الصارخ يجب أن يحول كيف نرى ونستخدم الثروة، مع إعطاء الأولوية لما نرسله للأمام على ما نراكمه.

concepts.title: False Security
concepts.coreInsight: Wealth creates an illusion of security and power in this life, but on the Day of Judgment, it offers no protection or benefit whatsoever.
concepts.whyItMatters: Recognizing wealth's limitations helps us avoid making it our ultimate goal, focusing instead on what truly matters eternally.
concepts.coreInsight_urdu: دولت اس زندگی میں سلامتی اور طاقت کا ایک وہم پیدا کرتی ہے، لیکن قیامت کے دن یہ کوئی تحفظ یا فائدہ نہیں دیتی۔
concepts.whyItMatters_urdu: دولت کی حدود کو پہچاننا ہمیں اسے اپنا حتمی مقصد بنانے سے بچاتا ہے، اس کی بجائے جو ابدی طور پر اہم ہے اس پر توجہ دیتے ہیں۔
concepts.coreInsight_ar: الثروة تخلق وهم الأمان والقوة في هذه الحياة، لكن في يوم القيامة، لا توفر أي حماية أو فائدة على الإطلاق.
concepts.whyItMatters_ar: إدراك قيود الثروة يساعدنا على تجنب جعلها هدفنا النهائي، مع التركيز بدلاً من ذلك على ما يهم حقاً أبدياً.

concepts.title: No Benefit
concepts.coreInsight: The phrase 'has not availed' (ma aghna) emphasizes total uselessness - wealth that seemed so powerful becomes completely powerless.
concepts.whyItMatters: This teaches us to invest in what benefits us eternally: good deeds, knowledge, and charity that follow us beyond the grave.
concepts.coreInsight_urdu: 'فائدہ نہیں دیا' کا جملہ مکمل بیکاری پر زور دیتا ہے - دولت جو اتنی طاقتور لگتی تھی بالکل بے طاقت ہو جاتی ہے۔
concepts.whyItMatters_urdu: یہ ہمیں سکھاتا ہے کہ وہ چیزیں جو ابدی طور پر فائدہ دیتی ہیں ان میں سرمایہ کاری کریں: نیک اعمال، علم، اور صدقہ جو قبر سے آگے ہمارے ساتھ جاتے ہیں۔
concepts.coreInsight_ar: عبارة 'ما أغنى' يؤكد على عدم الجدوى الكاملة - الثروة التي بدت قوية جداً تصبح عاجزة تماماً.
concepts.whyItMatters_ar: هذا يعلمنا الاستثمار فيما ينفعنا أبدياً: الأعمال الصالحة والعلم والصدقة التي تتبعنا ما بعد القبر.

28.layer4: Both Shia and Sunni scholars emphasize the uselessness of wealth on the Day of Judgment as described in this verse. Sunni exegetes like Ibn Kathir and Qurtubi explain that the lament about wealth not availing shows the person finally recognizes they wasted their life pursuing something temporary while neglecting eternal realities. Tabari emphasizes that wealth accumulated through exploitation and used selfishly becomes a source of regret rather than comfort. Sunni tradition includes many hadiths from Prophet Muhammad warning against attachment to wealth and emphasizing the importance of charity. Shia scholarship agrees with these fundamental teachings while adding particular emphasis on the obligation to support the righteous cause and the Ahlul Bayt. Allamah Tabatabai in Al-Mizan discusses how wealth represents a test of priorities, revealing whether a person values material security or divine pleasure. Tabrisi in Majma al-Bayan presents traditions from the Imams about the proper use of wealth and the severe accounting awaiting those who hoarded it or spent it in opposition to truth. Both traditions agree that this verse should inspire detachment from worldly wealth and generosity in spending for righteous causes. The shared message is that wealth should be a servant rather than a master, used as a tool for earning eternal reward.
28.layer4_urdu: شیعہ اور اہل سنت کے علما دولت کے عارضی ہونے پر متفق ہیں۔ ابن کثیر تفصیل دیتے ہیں۔ دونوں روایات بیان کرتی ہیں کہ دولت اہم نہیں۔
28.layer4_ar: يُؤكِّد علماء الشيعة والسنة عدم جدوى المال يوم القيامة كما تصفه هذه الآية. فمفسِّرو أهل السنة كابن كثير والقرطبي يُبيِّنون أن النواح على عدم إغناء المال يُظهر إدراك هذا الشخص الآن أنه أضاع حياته في مطاردة الزائل ومهمَل الأبدي. ويُؤكِّد الطبري أن المال المُكتسَب بالاستغلال والمُنفَق أنانيةً يصير مصدر ندم لا راحة. ويتضمَّن التراث السني أحاديث نبوية كثيرة تُحذِّر من التعلُّق بالمال وتُؤكِّد أهمية الصدقة. ويتفق التراث الشيعي مع هذه التعاليم الجوهرية مضيفاً تأكيداً خاصاً على واجب دعم الحق ونصرة أهل البيت عليهم السلام. والعلامة الطباطبائي في الميزان يُناقش كيف يُمثِّل المال اختبار الأولويات الكاشف هل يُقدِّم المرء الأمان المادي أم رضا الله. والشيخ الطبرسي في مجمع البيان يُورد روايات عن الأئمة في حُسن توظيف المال والحساب العسير المنتظر من يكتنزه أو يُنفقه في معارضة الحق. ويتفق التراثان على أن هذه الآية ينبغي أن تحثَّ المؤمنين على الانفكاك من الدنيا وتحرير الأيدي بالعطاء لأسباب البرِّ. والرسالة المشتركة أن المال ينبغي أن يكون خادماً لا سيِّداً، موظَّفاً أداةً لكسب الثواب الأبدي.
28.layer1: Verse twenty-eight records the condemned person's lament about the two things that defined their earthly existence and in which they placed their deepest trust: 'My wealth has not availed me! My power has perished from me!' In Arabic, the phrase ma aghna anni maliyah is structured as a rhetorical exclamation of uselessness: ma here is a particle of negation combined with astonishment, expressing that the very thing relied upon to provide security, to solve problems, to ward off harm, has done absolutely nothing. Maliyah, my wealth, ends with the familiar pause marker h, and the word aghna comes from ghina, meaning self-sufficiency, independence, the state of not needing help from others. The bitter irony is that wealth in this world appears to produce precisely this quality: the wealthy person appears self-sufficient, appears to need nothing, appears insulated from the vulnerabilities that afflict others. But in the moment that matters most, that appearance of self-sufficiency evaporates completely. The wealth that produced earthly independence produces zero independence from divine justice. The verse is thus a comprehensive demolition of wealth as a source of ultimate security. This is not an argument against wealth itself; the Quran elsewhere acknowledges wealth as a divine blessing when used righteously. It is an argument against placing ultimate trust in wealth, against allowing wealth to substitute for the relationship with Allah that alone provides genuine security. The second half of the verse, halaka anni sultaniyah, my power has perished from me, uses the word halaka, which is among the strongest Arabic words for destruction and annihilation. Power did not merely decrease or diminish; it perished, it was destroyed, it is gone as though it never existed. The word sultaniyah, my authority, can refer to any form of power: political authority, social influence, family connections, physical strength, or the authority of argument and persuasion. All of it has halaka, perished, in the face of divine judgment.
28.layer2: Ibn Kathir, in Tafsir al-Quran al-Azim, notes that the lament of verse twenty-eight is best understood in the context of those who made wealth and power their primary reliance in this world and their primary identity. He records the widespread view among the Salaf that this verse describes in particular the wealthy and powerful among the disbelievers of Mecca, who confidently wielded their wealth and authority against the Prophet and believed that these resources would always protect them. Ibn Kathir emphasises that maliyah in this context includes all material assets: gold, silver, land, trade goods, and any other form of worldly wealth. He also notes that the word aghna, to avail or to make self-sufficient, directly inverts the worldly experience of the wealthy: in this world, wealth seems to avail everything, to open every door, to solve every problem. On the Day of Judgment, this inversion becomes total. Al-Tabari, in Jami al-Bayan, records from Ibn Abbas and Mujahid that the phrase halaka anni sultaniyah refers to the complete loss of every instrument of worldly power, including wealth, kinship, tribal solidarity, political alliances, and physical force. Tabari notes that the word sultan can carry the meaning of proof or compelling argument in some Quranic contexts, and that some commentators interpreted this verse as the person confessing that they also lost their arguments: not only did their physical power perish but their ability to present any justification for their conduct also disappeared. Al-Qurtubi, in Al-Jami li-Ahkam al-Quran, draws the legal and ethical implications extensively, noting that this verse is among the Quran's strongest proofs for the obligation of spending wealth in Allah's path during one's lifetime. He argues that the person who sends their wealth forward through charitable giving in this world converts it from the maliyah of verse twenty-eight, which avails nothing on the Day of Judgment, into the bima aslaftum of verse twenty-four, which earns the feast of Paradise. Fakhr al-Din al-Razi, in Mafatih al-Ghayb, discusses the philosophical relationship between wealth, power, and the illusion of self-sufficiency, arguing that verse twenty-eight is the Quran's most compressed statement of why material security is ultimately illusory.
28.layer3: Wahbah al-Zuhayli, in Al-Tafsir al-Munir, reads verse twenty-eight as the culminating expression of a worldview that placed everything in the wrong objects of trust. He draws the contrast explicitly with verse twenty of the surah, where the person of the right hand confessed to living with zannantu, certainty about meeting their account, as the guiding principle of their life. The person of verse twenty-eight had instead lived with their wealth and their authority as the guiding principles: these were their zannantu, their certainty, their ground of security. And on the Day of Judgment, both have simultaneously perished. Al-Zuhayli observes that the specific combination of maliyah and sultaniyah in this verse is deliberately comprehensive: these two words between them cover the primary forms of worldly reliance available to human beings, material resources and social or political power. By presenting both as absolutely useless on the Day of Judgment, the Quran closes every apparent avenue of escape and makes unmistakable the lesson that divine accountability is answerable only by one's own personal record of faith and deeds. Sayyid Qutb, in Fi Zilal al-Quran, writes with characteristic power that verse twenty-eight is the Quran's most concentrated rebuttal of the worldview that equates success with wealth and power. He argues that the culture of the Quraysh, which the surah addresses in its Meccan context, is the same culture that dominates the contemporary world: a culture in which a person's worth is measured by their net worth and their influence, and in which those who possess neither are considered of little account. The surah strips away this entire value system in a single verse and reveals the nothingness that remains when the instruments of worldly dominance encounter the reality of divine justice. Sheikh Ibn Uthaymeen, commenting on this verse, pointed out the practical implications for the use of wealth in this life: the believer who gives generously in charity, who uses their authority to establish justice, who places their ultimate trust in Allah rather than in their bank account or social connections, is building toward the outcome of verses nineteen through twenty-four rather than the devastation of verse twenty-eight.

concepts.title: Lost Authority
concepts.coreInsight: The phrase 'Gone from me is my authority' reveals how all worldly power, status, and influence vanish completely on the Day of Judgment.
concepts.whyItMatters: Understanding that earthly authority is temporary helps us use power responsibly and humbly, knowing we answer to a Higher Authority.
concepts.coreInsight_urdu: 'میرا اقتدار مجھ سے چلا گیا' کا جملہ ظاہر کرتا ہے کہ تمام دنیاوی طاقت، حیثیت اور اثر و رسوخ قیامت کے دن مکمل طور پر ختم ہو جاتے ہیں۔
concepts.whyItMatters_urdu: یہ سمجھنا کہ دنیاوی اقتدار عارضی ہے، ہمیں طاقت کو ذمہ داری اور عاجزی سے استعمال کرنے میں مدد کرتا ہے، جانتے ہوئے کہ ہم ایک اعلیٰ اقتدار کے سامنے جوابدہ ہیں۔
concepts.coreInsight_ar: عبارة 'هلك عني سلطانيه' يكشف كيف تختفي كل القوة والمكانة والنفوذ الدنيوي تماماً في يوم القيامة.
concepts.whyItMatters_ar: فهم أن السلطة الأرضية مؤقتة يساعدنا على استخدام القوة بمسؤولية وتواضع، مع العلم أننا نجيب أمام سلطة أعلى.

concepts.title: Perished Influence
concepts.coreInsight: The word 'perished' (halaka) means destroyed or annihilated - authority doesn't just fade, it is completely obliterated before Allah's ultimate sovereignty.
concepts.whyItMatters: This reminds powerful people that their authority is a trust from Allah, to be used for justice and service, not oppression.
concepts.coreInsight_urdu: 'ہلاک' کا مطلب ہے تباہ یا نابود - اقتدار صرف ختم نہیں ہوتا، بلکہ اللہ کی حتمی بادشاہی کے سامنے مکمل طور پر ختم ہو جاتا ہے۔
concepts.whyItMatters_urdu: یہ طاقتور لوگوں کو یاد دلاتا ہے کہ ان کا اقتدار اللہ کی طرف سے امانت ہے، جسے انصاف اور خدمت کے لیے استعمال کرنا ہے، نہ کہ ظلم کے لیے۔
concepts.coreInsight_ar: كلمة 'هلك' تعني دُمر أو فُني - السلطة لا تتلاشى فقط، بل تُمحى تماماً أمام سيادة الله المطلقة.
concepts.whyItMatters_ar: هذا يذكر الأقوياء بأن سلطتهم أمانة من الله، لاستخدامها للعدل والخدمة، وليس للظلم.

concepts.title: Vanished Status
concepts.coreInsight: The 'authority' (sultan) refers to all forms of worldly status - political power, social influence, family connections, fame - all become worthless.
concepts.whyItMatters: True status comes from righteousness and divine acceptance, not from worldly position or social rank that vanishes at death.
concepts.coreInsight_urdu: 'اقتدار' دنیاوی حیثیت کی تمام شکلوں کا حوالہ دیتا ہے - سیاسی طاقت، سماجی اثر و رسوخ، خاندانی تعلقات، شہرت - سب بیکار ہو جاتے ہیں۔
concepts.whyItMatters_urdu: سچی حیثیت نیکی اور الٰہی قبولیت سے آتی ہے، نہ کہ دنیاوی مقام یا سماجی درجے سے جو موت پر ختم ہو جاتے ہیں۔
concepts.coreInsight_ar: 'السلطان' يشير إلى جميع أشكال المكانة الدنيوية - القوة السياسية، النفوذ الاجتماعي، العلاقات العائلية، الشهرة - كلها تصبح لا قيمة لها.
concepts.whyItMatters_ar: المكانة الحقيقية تأتي من الصلاح والقبول الإلهي، وليس من الموقع الدنيوي أو الرتبة الاجتماعية التي تختفي عند الموت.

29.layer4: Both Shia and Sunni scholars interpret this verse as describing the complete powerlessness of the condemned on Judgment Day, regardless of their worldly status. Sunni exegetes like Ibn Kathir and Tabari explain that the loss of authority shows that worldly power provides no protection against divine judgment and that all human authority is temporary. Qurtubi emphasizes that this lament comes from those who relied on their power and position rather than on righteousness and divine mercy. Sunni tradition includes many warnings from Prophet Muhammad about the heavy responsibility of leadership and the severe accounting awaiting those who abuse authority. Shia scholarship agrees with these fundamental interpretations while placing particular emphasis on the illegitimate usurpation of authority from the rightfully appointed Imams. Allamah Tabatabai in Al-Mizan discusses how worldly authority often corrupts those who possess it, leading them to believe in their own power rather than recognizing their dependence on Allah. Tabrisi in Majma al-Bayan presents traditions from the Ahlul Bayt specifically condemning those who seized authority that belonged to the Prophet's family and those who followed such usurpers. This represents a significant interpretive difference, with Shia exegesis applying the verse particularly to historical conflicts over legitimate leadership. Both traditions agree that the verse warns against pursuit of power for its own sake and emphasizes the responsibility of using authority justly.
29.layer4_urdu: شیعہ اور اہل سنت کے علما طاقت کے عارضی ہونے پر متفق ہیں۔ ابن کثیر تفصیل دیتے ہیں۔ دونوں روایات بیان کرتی ہیں کہ الله کی طاقت ہی حقیقی ہے۔
29.layer4_ar: يتفق علماء الشيعة والسنة على تفسير هذه الآية بوصفها تصويراً للعجز المطلق للمحكوم عليهم يوم القيامة بصرف النظر عن مكانتهم الدنيوية. فمفسِّرو أهل السنة كابن كثير والطبري يُبيِّنون أن ضياع السلطان يُجلِّي أن القوة الدنيوية لا تُغني عن العذاب الإلهي وأن كل سلطة بشرية عرَضٌ زائل. ويُؤكِّد القرطبي أن هذا النواح يصدر عمَّن اتَّكلوا على نفوذهم ومواقعهم بدلاً من التقوى ورحمة الله. ويتضمَّن التراث السني تحذيرات نبوية كثيرة من ثقل مسؤولية القيادة والحساب العسير المنتظر من يُسيء استخدام السلطة. ويتفق التراث الشيعي مع هذه التفسيرات الجوهرية مُضيفاً تأكيداً خاصاً على اغتصاب الولاية الشرعية من الأئمة المعيَّنين من الله. والعلامة الطباطبائي في الميزان يُناقش كيف تُفسد السلطة الدنيوية في الغالب أصحابها فتُوهمهم بالاعتداد بأنفسهم بدلاً من إدراك افتقارهم إلى الله. والشيخ الطبرسي في مجمع البيان يُورد روايات عن أهل البيت تُدين بصفة خاصة من اغتصبوا الإرث الشرعي لآل النبي وأتباعهم. وهذا يُمثِّل فارقاً تفسيرياً بارزاً إذ يُطبِّق التفسير الشيعي الآية بصفة خاصة على نزاعات تاريخية حول الولاية الشرعية. ويتفق التراثان على أن الآية تُحذِّر من السعي وراء السلطة لذاتها وتُؤكِّد وجوب توظيفها بعدل وأمانة.
29.layer1: Verse twenty-nine is the culmination of the condemned person's self-expressed lament, and it completes the picture that verse twenty-eight began. The full statement across the two verses reads: 'My wealth has not availed me! My power has perished from me!' These are the two pillars of worldly identity that have both collapsed simultaneously. Having established in verse twenty-eight the uselessness of wealth, verse twenty-nine drives home the uselessness of authority and power with the word halaka, perished, which is even more forceful than ma aghna, 'has not availed.' Sultaniyah, my authority or my power, encompasses not only political or governmental authority but any kind of dominance or influence over others. In the culture of seventh-century Arabia, this would have included tribal authority, the authority of wealth over dependents, the authority of age and reputation, and the authority of physical strength. In any cultural context, sultan represents the capacity to make things happen, to compel outcomes, to bend the world to one's will. All of that has halaka, perished, in the most complete and irreversible sense. The symmetry of the two verses is striking: verse twenty-eight uses ma aghna, a verb of providing benefit, and verse twenty-nine uses halaka, a verb of total destruction. The two together cover both dimensions of what power and wealth were supposed to offer: they were supposed to be beneficial in times of need, and they were supposed to be robust and durable. On the Day of Judgment, both properties have simultaneously failed. They could not provide benefit and they could not endure. This is the Quranic verdict on every form of worldly security that is not grounded in the relationship with Allah: not merely insufficient but completely hollow, a source of false comfort in this life and a source of bitter regret in the next.
29.layer2: Ibn Kathir, in Tafsir al-Quran al-Azim, addresses the two verses together as a unit and notes that the scholars of the classical period identified the condemned person in this passage as a composite portrait drawing on specific individuals among the Quraysh who were known for their wealth and authority and who used both in opposition to Islam. He mentions that some commentators identified the portrait with Abu Jahl or with Umayyah ibn Khalaf, both wealthy and powerful opponents of the Prophet whose wealth and authority ultimately profited them nothing. Ibn Kathir emphasises, however, that the Quran's language is universal rather than specific: the condemned person is not named because the portrait is intended to apply to any person in any time who places their ultimate reliance in wealth and power rather than in faith and righteous action. Al-Tabari, in Jami al-Bayan, records the interpretations of multiple scholars on the word sultaniyah, noting that while the most common view understands it as referring to worldly power and authority, some of the Successors including Mujahid interpreted it as referring specifically to the arguments and proofs that the person attempted to use in their defence, suggesting that on the Day of Judgment not only physical power but the capacity for reasoned self-justification also collapses completely. Al-Qurtubi, in Al-Jami li-Ahkam al-Quran, connects this verse to the extensive Quranic theme of the abolition of all forms of intercessory power and authority on the Day of Judgment, citing the verse that 'no soul shall benefit from the intercession of another on that day' and noting that verse twenty-nine is the experiential, first-person version of that Quranic principle. Fakhr al-Din al-Razi, in Mafatih al-Ghayb, notes the profound literary effect of juxtaposing ma aghna with halaka: the first expresses the uselessness of wealth in the present tense, as an ongoing failure to provide what was expected, while halaka expresses the destruction of authority as a completed past event, something already annihilated. This temporal distinction gives the lament a devastating completeness: wealth is still failing in the present and authority has already been destroyed in the past.
29.layer3: Wahbah al-Zuhayli, in Al-Tafsir al-Munir, draws the contemporary lesson from verse twenty-nine with particular force, noting that the twin failure of maliyah and sultaniyah in these two verses maps directly onto the two primary sources of security that modern culture offers as substitutes for genuine faith: financial wealth and social or political power. He observes that the entire architecture of modern secular society is built on the premise that these two things, if accumulated in sufficient quantities, provide the security, meaning, and protection that human beings need. The surah demolishes this premise in two verses, showing that on the day that truly matters, both fail completely and simultaneously, leaving the person with nothing but the record of their personal choices and the quality of their relationship with their Creator. Sayyid Qutb, in Fi Zilal al-Quran, writes that verses twenty-eight and twenty-nine constitute the Quran's most direct address to the culture of the wealthy and powerful, which in his reading includes both the Meccan merchants who opposed the Prophet and the dominant cultures of the contemporary world. He argues that the surah is addressed precisely to those who would say 'my wealth protects me' and 'my authority secures me,' and that these two verses strip away the facade of security with surgical precision. He connects this to the Islamic understanding of tawakkul, complete reliance on Allah, arguing that the believer who practises genuine tawakkul in this world is protected against the catastrophe of verses twenty-eight and twenty-nine, because they never made wealth or authority the foundation of their security in the first place. Sheikh Ibn Uthaymeen, in his reflection on these verses, noted that the cry halaka anni sultaniyah is the precise opposite of the takbir, Allahu Akbar, which the believer pronounces in prayer. The believer's takbir declares that Allah is greater than everything else, including wealth and power. The condemned person's lament in verse twenty-nine confesses that they forgot this truth throughout their life and are confronting its consequences only now, when it is too late.

concepts.title: Divine Seizure
concepts.coreInsight: Allah's direct command 'Seize him' marks the moment when divine mercy ends and justice begins - the condemned is taken into custody for punishment.
concepts.whyItMatters: This terrifying command serves as the ultimate warning to repent while we can, before the door of mercy closes forever.
concepts.coreInsight_urdu: اللہ کا براہ راست حکم 'اسے پکڑو' اس لمحے کی نشاندہی کرتا ہے جب الٰہی رحمت ختم ہوتی ہے اور انصاف شروع ہوتا ہے - مجرم کو سزا کے لیے حراست میں لیا جاتا ہے۔
concepts.whyItMatters_urdu: یہ خوفناک حکم حتمی تنبیہ ہے کہ توبہ کریں جب ہم کر سکتے ہیں، اس سے پہلے کہ رحمت کا دروازہ ہمیشہ کے لیے بند ہو جائے۔
concepts.coreInsight_ar: أمر الله المباشر 'خذوه' يمثل اللحظة التي تنتهي فيها الرحمة الإلهية ويبدأ العدل - يُؤخذ المدان للعقاب.
concepts.whyItMatters_ar: هذا الأمر المرعب يعمل كتحذير نهائي للتوبة بينما نستطيع، قبل أن يُغلق باب الرحمة إلى الأبد.

concepts.title: Bound in Chains
concepts.coreInsight: The command to 'shackle him' (faghulluhu) indicates restraint and helplessness - the sinner who was free to sin is now bound in punishment.
concepts.whyItMatters: The freedom we have now to choose between right and wrong is temporary - how we use this freedom determines our eternal state.
concepts.coreInsight_urdu: 'اسے جکڑ دو' کا حکم پابندی اور بے بسی کی نشاندہی کرتا ہے - گناہ گار جو گناہ کرنے میں آزاد تھا اب سزا میں جکڑا ہوا ہے۔
concepts.whyItMatters_urdu: ہمیں اب جو آزادی ہے صحیح اور غلط کے درمیان انتخاب کرنے کی وہ عارضی ہے - ہم اس آزادی کو کیسے استعمال کرتے ہیں یہ ہماری ابدی حالت کا تعین کرتا ہے۔
concepts.coreInsight_ar: أمر 'فغلوه' يشير للقيد والعجز - الخاطئ الذي كان حراً في الإثم أصبح الآن مقيداً في العقاب.
concepts.whyItMatters_ar: الحرية التي لدينا الآن للاختيار بين الصواب والخطأ مؤقتة - كيف نستخدم هذه الحرية يحدد حالتنا الأبدية.

concepts.title: Angels of Justice
concepts.coreInsight: The angels commanded to seize and shackle are the executors of divine justice - they implement Allah's judgment with perfect obedience.
concepts.whyItMatters: The same angels who protect believers become instruments of punishment for the wicked, showing that divine mercy and justice are two sides of one reality.
concepts.coreInsight_urdu: پکڑنے اور جکڑنے کا حکم پانے والے فرشتے الٰہی انصاف کے نفاذ کنندہ ہیں - وہ اللہ کے فیصلے کو کامل فرمانبرداری سے نافذ کرتے ہیں۔
concepts.whyItMatters_urdu: وہی فرشتے جو مومنین کی حفاظت کرتے ہیں برائی کرنے والوں کے لیے سزا کے آلہ بن جاتے ہیں، یہ دکھاتے ہوئے کہ الٰہی رحمت اور انصاف ایک ہی حقیقت کے دو پہلو ہیں۔
concepts.coreInsight_ar: الملائكة المأمورون بالقبض والتقييد هم منفذو العدل الإلهي - ينفذون حكم الله بطاعة كاملة.
concepts.whyItMatters_ar: نفس الملائكة الذين يحمون المؤمنين يصبحون أدوات للعقاب للأشرار، مما يظهر أن الرحمة والعدل الإلهيين وجهان لحقيقة واحدة.

30.layer4: Both Shia and Sunni scholars interpret this verse as describing the beginning of punishment for those condemned to Hellfire. Sunni exegetes like Ibn Kathir and Tabari explain that the command to seize and shackle is given to the angels of punishment, who will bind the condemned and drag them to Hell. Qurtubi emphasizes that this verse shows the certainty and severity of divine punishment, which is executed swiftly without delay or reprieve once judgment is rendered. Sunni tradition generally applies this to disbelievers and severe sinners facing damnation. Shia scholarship agrees with the fundamental interpretation while placing particular emphasis on those who opposed the rightful Imams and led others astray from the true path. Allamah Tabatabai in Al-Mizan discusses how the shackling represents being bound by one's own deeds, which become physical restraints in the Hereafter. Tabrisi in Majma al-Bayan presents traditions from the Ahlul Bayt about specific categories of people who will face this command, particularly oppressive rulers and religious hypocrites who misled people while claiming to guide them. Both traditions agree that this verse serves as a severe warning to examine our lives and ensure we are following the path that leads to salvation rather than damnation. The shared message is that divine punishment is real and inescapable for those who die in a state of rejection of truth.
30.layer4_urdu: شیعہ اور سنی دونوں علماء اس آیت کو ان لوگوں کے عذاب کی شروعات کے طور پر تشریح کرتے ہیں جو جہنم میں سزا پانے والے ہیں۔ سنی مفسرین جیسے ابن کثیر اور طبری وضاحت کرتے ہیں کہ فرشتوں کو یہ حکم دیا جاتا ہے کہ وہ مذموم لوگوں کو پکڑیں اور جہنم میں رکھیں۔ قرطبی تاکید کرتے ہیں کہ یہ آیت الہی عذاب کی یقینیت اور سختی کو ظاہر کرتی ہے۔ شیعہ علمیہ سنی عالمین سے متفق ہے کہ بنیادی تشریح میں تھوڑا سا فرق ہے - سنی تفسیر مختلف لوگوں کی وسیع تر اقسام پر لاگو ہوتی ہے جب کہ شیعہ علماء خاص طور پر ان پر زور دیتے ہیں جنہوں نے صحیح اماموں کے حقوق کا انکار کیا۔
30.layer4_ar: يتفق علماء الشيعة والسنة على تفسير هذه الآية بوصفها تصويراً لبدء العقوبة على المحكوم عليهم بالنار. فمفسِّرو أهل السنة كابن كثير والطبري يُبيِّنون أن أمر الأخذ والتغليل موجَّه إلى ملائكة العذاب التي ستُقيِّد المحكوم عليهم وتسحبهم إلى جهنَّم. ويُؤكِّد القرطبي أن هذه الآية تُجلِّي حتمية عقوبة الله وشدَّتها التي تُنفَّذ بسرعة لا تأخير فيها ولا إمهال متى صدر الحكم. والعلامة الطباطبائي في الميزان يُناقش كيف يُمثِّل التغليل تقييداً بالأعمال ذاتها التي تصير في الآخرة قيوداً جسدية. والشيخ الطبرسي في مجمع البيان يُورد روايات عن أهل البيت في فئات بعينها ستواجه هذا الأمر، ولا سيَّما الحكَّام الظالمون والمنافقون الدينيون الذين أضلُّوا الناس بدعوى هدايتهم. ويُضيف التراث الشيعي تأكيداً خاصاً على من عارضوا الأئمة الشرعيين وأضلُّوا الأمة عن الصراط الحق. ويتفق التراثان على أن الآية تُقدِّم إنذاراً بالغ الحدَّة بمراجعة حياتنا وضمان انتهاجنا الطريق المُفضي إلى النجاة لا إلى الهلاك. والرسالة المشتركة أن العقاب الإلهي واقع لا مهرب منه لمن يموتون على رفض الحق، وأن وقت التوبة والعمل الصالح الآن قبل فوات الأوان.
30.layer1: With verse thirty, the surah shifts from the first-person lament of the condemned person to the direct divine command that initiates their punishment. The voice of the doomed individual falls silent and the voice of Allah commands: 'Seize him and shackle him.' The shift is sudden and total. One moment we are hearing the desperate cries of someone lamenting the uselessness of their wealth and the perishing of their authority; the next moment Allah commands the angels with two terse imperatives: khudzuhu, seize him, and ghulluhu, shackle him. There is no deliberation, no debate, no last-minute appeal. The judgment has been rendered, the record has been given in the left hand, the account has been presented, and now the execution of justice begins. The word khudzuhu, seize him, comes from the root akhadha, meaning to take firm hold of something, to grip it decisively and completely. The angels do not gently escort the condemned; they seize. The word ghulluhu, shackle him, comes from ghull, meaning a collar or fetter placed around the neck, restraining movement and signifying total captivity. In this life, the condemned person wielded their authority freely, moved without restraint, did as they pleased. Now the freedom of this world is replaced by the restraint of divine justice. The practical implication of this verse for believers reading it in this world is direct and sobering: the freedom of movement, the freedom of choice, the freedom to repent and change that characterises life in this world will not always be available. There is a moment, described in verse thirty, when that freedom ends and divine justice takes over without delay. The urgency is not a reason for despair but for decisive action: use the freedom of this world, the freedom to choose, to repent, to give, to worship, before the moment described in verse thirty arrives.
30.layer2: Ibn Kathir, in Tafsir al-Quran al-Azim, explains that the command khudzuhu, seize him, is addressed to the angels of punishment who are assigned to carry out the sentences of divine justice on the Day of Judgment. He records that some of the scholars of the Salaf, including Qatadah and others preserved in the chains of Al-Tabari, understood the command as being given publicly before the assembled gathering of all creation on the Day of Judgment, heightening the condemned person's humiliation. Ibn Kathir notes that the shackling of ghulluhu is confirmed by authentic hadith to be a literal physical restraint in the Hereafter, citing the hadith in Sahih Muslim that describes the condemned being bound with chains of fire. He also draws attention to the economy of the command: two words, khudzuhu and ghulluhu, express the entirety of the transition from condemnation to punishment, which reflects the Quranic principle that divine command requires nothing more than the word to be executed. Al-Tabari, in Jami al-Bayan, records from Ibn Abbas that the order of the commands in verses thirty through thirty-two, seize, shackle, then drive into Hell, then chain with a seventy-cubit chain, represents a deliberate sequence of escalating punishment rather than a single simultaneous action. The punishment is staged and progressive, with each stage compounding the previous one, a narrative technique that maximises the weight of the description and makes the reality of the punishment vivid to the listener. Al-Qurtubi, in Al-Jami li-Ahkam al-Quran, draws the theological lesson that the directness and immediacy of the command in verse thirty establishes without ambiguity that there is no arbitration, no delay, no final chance for plea, once the judgment of the Day of Judgment has been rendered. This is distinct from the justice of this world, where appeals and delays are possible; the justice of Allah on the Day of Judgment is instantaneous and irrevocable. Fakhr al-Din al-Razi notes that the shift from the first-person lament of the condemned in verses twenty-five through twenty-nine to the divine command of verse thirty is itself a theological statement: the condemned person's voice, which dominated the preceding verses, is now simply overridden by the divine command, illustrating the complete supremacy of divine authority over all human speech, argument, and will.
30.layer3: Wahbah al-Zuhayli, in Al-Tafsir al-Munir, focuses on the structural significance of verse thirty as a pivot point in the surah. He notes that the surah has spent verses twenty-five through twenty-nine entirely within the perspective of the condemned person, giving extended space to their laments and confessions. This extended space is itself an act of the surah's eloquence: it allows the reader to fully inhabit the condemned person's perspective, to feel the weight of their regret, before the divine command of verse thirty abruptly and definitively closes that space. The condemned person's perspective ceases at exactly the moment that divine justice begins, and that simultaneity is itself the deepest lesson: the opportunity for self-expression, self-determination, and self-advocacy exists only within the window of this world. Once that window closes, as verse thirty illustrates, the divine command takes over entirely. Al-Zuhayli connects this to the Islamic emphasis on the urgency of repentance: every moment in which a person is still alive is a moment in which they still possess the freedom that the condemned person in verse thirty has permanently lost. Sayyid Qutb, in Fi Zilal al-Quran, writes that the two-word command of verse thirty, khudzuhu ghulluhu, is among the most frightening phrases in the Quran precisely because of its absolute terseness. There is no explanation, no elaboration, no softening qualifier. The command is given and it will be executed. Qutb argues that this terseness is itself a rhetorical and theological statement: the condemned person's laments occupied five full verses, while the divine command requires only two words. The contrast in length mirrors the contrast in power: all the human eloquence of verses twenty-five through twenty-nine amounts to nothing against the two words of verse thirty. Sheikh Ibn Uthaymeen, in his commentary, drew the lesson that verse thirty is the logical endpoint of a life lived without the zannantu of verse twenty. The person who lived with genuine certainty about their account prepared for this moment throughout their life by building a record worthy of the right hand. The person who lived without that certainty is seized in verse thirty unprepared, unprotected, and with nothing to offer but the record they accumulated in heedlessness.

concepts.title: Divine Command
concepts.coreInsight: The imperative 'salluhu' (drive him) is a direct command to the angels of Hell, showing the severity and inevitability of punishment for those who rejected Allah's truth.
concepts.whyItMatters: This stark command reveals that entry into Hellfire is not accidental but a deliberate consequence of choices made in worldly life, executed by divine decree.
concepts.coreInsight_urdu: امر 'صلّوہ' (اسے ڈالو) جہنم کے فرشتوں کو براہ راست حکم ہے، ان لوگوں کے لیے سزا کی شدت اور ناگزیریت کو ظاہر کرتا ہے جنہوں نے اللہ کی سچائی کو مسترد کیا۔
concepts.whyItMatters_urdu: یہ سخت حکم ظاہر کرتا ہے کہ جہنم میں داخلہ حادثاتی نہیں بلکہ دنیاوی زندگی میں کیے گئے انتخاب کا جان بوجھ کر نتیجہ ہے، الہی فرمان کے ذریعے عمل میں لایا گیا۔
concepts.coreInsight_ar: الأمر 'صلّوه' (ادفعوه) هو أمر مباشر لملائكة جهنم، يُظهر شدة وحتمية العقاب لمن رفض حقيقة الله.
concepts.whyItMatters_ar: هذا الأمر الصارم يكشف أن دخول جهنم ليس عرضيًا بل نتيجة متعمدة للاختيارات المتخذة في الحياة الدنيوية، منفذة بمرسوم إلهي.

concepts.title: Blazing Torment
concepts.coreInsight: Al-Jahim refers to the intensely blazing fire, one of Hell's specific names emphasizing its scorching, all-consuming nature that burns both body and soul.
concepts.whyItMatters: Understanding Hell's reality as literal fire, not metaphor, should create genuine fear (khawf) that motivates us to avoid the sins that lead there.
concepts.coreInsight_urdu: الجحیم شدید بھڑکتی آگ کا حوالہ دیتا ہے، جہنم کے مخصوص ناموں میں سے ایک جو اس کی جھلسا دینے والی، سب کچھ کھا جانے والی نوعیت پر زور دیتا ہے جو جسم اور روح دونوں کو جلاتی ہے۔
concepts.whyItMatters_urdu: جہنم کی حقیقت کو لفظی آگ کے طور پر سمجھنا، استعارہ نہیں، حقیقی خوف (خوف) پیدا کرنا چاہیے جو ہمیں ان گناہوں سے بچنے کی ترغیب دے جو وہاں لے جاتے ہیں۔
concepts.coreInsight_ar: الجحيم يشير إلى النار الملتهبة بشدة، أحد أسماء جهنم المحددة التي تؤكد على طبيعتها المحرقة الآكلة التي تحرق الجسد والروح معًا.
concepts.whyItMatters_ar: فهم واقع جهنم كنار حرفية، وليس استعارة، يجب أن يخلق خوفًا حقيقيًا (خوف) يحفزنا على تجنب الخطايا التي تؤدي إليها.

concepts.title: Sequential Punishment
concepts.coreInsight: Thumma (then) indicates progression through stages of punishment - first seizing (v.30), then driving into fire (v.31), then chaining (v.32), each escalating in severity.
concepts.whyItMatters: This staged progression shows that punishment in Hell is methodical and inescapable, moving from capture to confinement to eternal torment.
concepts.coreInsight_urdu: ثم (پھر) سزا کے مراحل سے گزرنے کی نشاندہی کرتا ہے - پہلے پکڑنا (آیت 30)، پھر آگ میں ڈالنا (آیت 31)، پھر زنجیریں (آیت 32)، ہر ایک شدت میں بڑھتا ہوا۔
concepts.whyItMatters_urdu: یہ مرحلہ وار ترقی ظاہر کرتی ہے کہ جہنم میں سزا طریقہ کار اور ناگزیر ہے، گرفتاری سے قید سے ابدی عذاب تک منتقل ہوتی ہے۔
concepts.coreInsight_ar: ثم (ثم) يشير إلى التقدم عبر مراحل العقاب - أولاً القبض (الآية 30)، ثم الدفع إلى النار (الآية 31)، ثم التقييد (الآية 32)، كل منها يتصاعد في الشدة.
concepts.whyItMatters_ar: هذا التقدم المرحلي يُظهر أن العقاب في جهنم منهجي ولا مفر منه، ينتقل من القبض إلى الحبس إلى العذاب الأبدي.

31.layer4: Both Shia and Sunni commentators agree that this verse describes the punishment for persistent disbelief and neglect of social duties. Ibn Kathir and other Sunni scholars emphasize the sequence of punishments and their severity as divine justice. Tabari notes the active role of angels in executing Allah's commands. However, Shia scholars like Tabatabai give particular emphasis to the social justice dimension, connecting the theological crime of disbelief with the practical crime of abandoning the poor. This reflects the Shia emphasis on the interconnection of faith and righteous action as exemplified by the Ahlul Bayt. Sunni commentator Al-Razi focuses more on the divine attributes of justice and power demonstrated in these verses. Both traditions agree that the punishment described is real, severe, and eternal for unrepentant disbelievers. The scholarly consensus across both traditions is that these verses serve as serious warning and motivation for believers to maintain both sound belief and charitable conduct throughout their lives.
31.layer4_urdu: شیعہ اور سنی دونوں مفسرین سمجھتے ہیں کہ یہ آیت ایمان کی ہٹ دھرمی سے انکار اور سماجی فرائض کی نظر انداری کے لیے عذاب کو بیان کرتی ہے۔ ابن کثیر اور دیگر سنی علماء عذاب کی ترتیب اور اس کی سختی پر زور دیتے ہیں جو الہی انصاف ہے۔ شیعہ علماء جیسے طباطبائی سماجی انصاف کے پہلو کو خاص زور دیتے ہیں، جو اہل بیت کی تعلیمات میں ایمان اور راست کاری کا باہمی تعلق ظاہر کرتا ہے۔ دونوں روایات متفق ہیں کہ قیامت کا دن لوگوں کو ان کے ایمان اور عادل سلوک کے لیے سوال کریں گا۔
31.layer4_ar: يتَّفق علماء الشيعة والسنة على أن هذه الآية تصف العقوبة على الكفر المستديم والتقصير في الواجبات الاجتماعية. فابن كثير وغيره من علماء السنة يُؤكِّدون تتالي العقوبات وشدَّتها باعتبارها عدلاً إلهياً. ويُلاحِظ الطبري الدور الفاعل للملائكة في تنفيذ أوامر الله. غير أن علماء الشيعة كالطباطبائي يُولون أهمية خاصة للبعد الاجتماعي العادل في هذه العقوبة، إذ يربطون الجريمة العقدية المتمثِّلة في الكفر بالجريمة العملية المتمثِّلة في إهمال الفقراء. وهذا يعكس التأكيد الشيعي على الترابط بين الإيمان والعمل الصالح كما جسَّده أهل البيت عليهم السلام في سيرتهم العملية. ويُركِّز المفسِّر السني الرازي على الصفات الإلهية للعدل والقدرة الظاهرة في هذه الآيات. ويتَّفق كلا التراثين على أن العقوبة المذكورة حقيقية وشديدة وأبدية في حق الكافرين غير التائبين. والإجماع العلمي في التراثين معاً أن هذه الآيات تُقدِّم تحذيراً بالغاً ودافعاً قوياً للمؤمنين للمثابرة على صحَّة الاعتقاد وحُسن الخُلق والإنفاق في سبيل الله طوال الحياة.
31.layer1: Verse thirty-one continues the escalating divine command that began in verse thirty with the order to seize and shackle the condemned. Now comes the third imperative: salluhu al-jahim, drive him into the Blazing Fire. The word salluhu comes from the root sala, meaning to expose something directly to fire, to thrust it into the flames. It is not a passive entry but an active, forceful driving into the fire, executed by the angels of punishment in obedience to the divine command. Al-Jahim is one of the Quranic names for Hell, specifically emphasizing the intensity of its heat and the roaring, raging nature of its flames. The name comes from the root jahama, referring to fire so fierce and blazing that it has a visible depth and intensity. Throughout the Quran, different names are used for the Hereafter's punishment, and Al-Jahim is among the most vivid, conveying not just the fact of fire but the overwhelming, all-consuming quality of its burning. The structural sequence across verses thirty through thirty-two is deliberate and powerful: seize, shackle, then throw into Hellfire. Each command builds on the last, moving the condemned person step by step from capture to restraint to the final destination of punishment. The particle thumma, meaning then, between verse thirty and verse thirty-one, and between thirty-one and thirty-two, indicates a sequence with deliberate staging rather than all occurring at once. For the believer reading this verse in the present life, the implication is profound: the entry into Al-Jahim is not sudden and arbitrary but the logical endpoint of a journey that began with choices made in this world. Every day in this life is a day in which the path to Al-Jahim can be exchanged for a different destination, through sincere faith, repentance, and righteous action.
31.layer2: Ibn Kathir, in Tafsir al-Quran al-Azim, comments on the command salluhu al-jahim by noting that it is the climax of the divine orders given to the angels of punishment following the initial commands of seizing and shackling in verse thirty. He explains that the verb sala, from which salluhu derives, specifically means to expose directly to fire, and that this direct exposure to Al-Jahim is the culmination of the judgment rendered against the condemned person whose record was given in their left hand. Ibn Kathir also notes the significance of the name Al-Jahim, observing that it is one of the seven levels of Hell mentioned in Islamic tradition, and that its use here emphasizes the ferocity and depth of the fire into which the condemned is driven. Al-Tabari, in Jami al-Bayan, records from the early Salaf including Qatadah and Ibn Abbas that the sequence of commands across verses thirty through thirty-two is intended to convey a progressive and staged punishment, with each element, the seizure, the shackling, and the driving into the fire, representing a distinct phase of the execution of divine justice on the Day of Judgment. Al-Tabari himself notes that the active nature of the verb in salluhu, its command form addressed to the angels, emphasizes that this is not a passive state into which the condemned falls but an active punishment carried out by created beings in obedience to their Creator. Al-Qurtubi, in Al-Jami li-Ahkam al-Quran, draws attention to the rhetorical economy of the entire sequence: three commands across three verses accomplish the complete description of the transition from condemnation to punishment, and each command is a single word in Arabic, reflecting the absolute efficiency of divine will when it translates into action. The brevity of the commands, khudzuhu, ghulluhu, salluhu, contrasts sharply with the extended laments of the condemned person in verses twenty-five through twenty-nine, a contrast that itself teaches that all the eloquence of the condemned amounts to nothing before the single words of divine command.
31.layer3: Wahbah al-Zuhayli, in Al-Tafsir al-Munir, reads verse thirty-one as completing the transition from description to execution that began with verse thirty. He notes that the three-verse sequence of commands, seize, shackle, drive into Hellfire, represents the Quran's most concentrated depiction of divine justice being administered, and that the economy and directness of each command is itself a theological statement about the nature of that justice: it is precise, immediate, and executed without any of the ambiguity or delay that human systems of justice inevitably introduce. Al-Zuhayli also observes that the name Al-Jahim carries a specific connotation of a fire that has depth and intensity, and that the use of this particular name for Hell in this verse, rather than simply al-nar, the fire, adds a layer of vivid specificity to the punishment described. Sayyid Qutb, in Fi Zilal al-Quran, writes that the command salluhu al-jahim is among the most terrifying phrases in the Quran because of its complete finality. The condemned person has cried out in verse twenty-five, lamented their ignorance in verse twenty-six, wished for death in verse twenty-seven, been reminded of their wealth and authority in verse twenty-eight and twenty-nine, and then in verse thirty the divine command began and their voice ceased entirely. In verse thirty-one, the second of three commands drives them further along a path from which there is absolutely no return. Qutb argues that the starkness of this moment should be felt deeply by every reader, because it is the logical destination of a life spent without genuine faith and without practical compassion toward the poor, which the following verses identify as the twin crimes of the condemned.
